be Jointly Optimized

Ryuto Koike1

Abstract
Detecting machine-generated text is essential for transparency and account-
ability when deploying large language models (LLMs). Among detection
approaches, watermarking is a statistically reliable method by design—it
embeds detectable signals into LLM outputs by biasing their token dis-
tributions. However, it has been reported that watermarked LLMs often
perform worse on downstream tasks. We propose PUPPET, a framework
that fine-tunes an LLM via reinforcement learning to generate text that is
both more detectable and better performing on downstream tasks. We use
two reward functions: a detector that outputs a machine-class likelihood
and an evaluator that measures a task-specific metric. Experiments on
long-form QA, summarization, and essay writing show that LLMs trained
with PUPPET achieve high detectability competitive with watermarking
methods while outperforming them on downstream tasks. The analysis
shows that this optimization can be performed efficiently with only a few
thousand samples in 1–2 GPU hours. Moreover, these gains are consistent
across out-of-domain tasks, different LLM families, and model sizes, and
are even robust to paraphrasing attacks.
1
Introduction
LLMs now generate so fluent text that humans are almost unable to distinguish it from
human-written text (Wang et al., 2025b; Clark et al., 2021; Jakesch et al., 2023). This raises
urgent concerns about misuse, including academic fraud, spam, and automated disin-
formation campaigns (Chen & Shu, 2024; Goldstein et al., 2023). Therefore, detecting
machine-generated text is essential for transparency and accountability.
From a LLM provider’s perspective, it is ideal for LLMs to be both highly detectable and
strong on downstream tasks: high detectability supports accountability and misuse tracking,
while strong task performance prevents users from exploring less detectable alternatives.
Watermarking (Kirchenbauer et al., 2023) is the de facto standard approach toward this goal—
by biasing token distributions at generation time, it enables statistically reliable detection
via a hypothesis test with a provably controlled false-positive rate. However, since this
approach optimizes only detectability, the resulting output distribution deviates from what
is optimal for downstream tasks, leading to task performance degradation (Ajith et al., 2024;
Fu et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025a; Fernandez et al., 2023). Directly optimizing the LLM for
both detectability and task performance simultaneously would address this limitation.
In this paper, we propose PUPPET
, a framework for training an LLM via Direct Preference
Optimization (DPO; Rafailov et al. (2023)) to produce texts that are both more detectable
and better performing on downstream tasks. We use two reward functions: a detector
that outputs a machine-generated class likelihood, and an evaluator that measures task
performance. The detector encourages outputs that exhibit features indicative of machine-
generated text, while the evaluator encourages the model to produce outputs that improve

major challenge for watermarking methods. In addition, PUPPET is practically efficient,
requiring only a few thousand samples and 1–2 GPU hours. Finally, our exploratory analysis
suggests that the learned detection-relevant features may also support model attribution,
i.e., identifying whether a given LLM has been trained with PUPPET.

Experimental Setup
Datasets Q
We use three datasets spanning diverse text-generation tasks: ELI5 (long-form
QA; Fan et al. (2019); Guo et al. (2023)) and Multi-News (summarization; Fabbri et al.
(2019)) from WaterBench (Tu et al., 2024), which is a standard benchmark for evaluating
watermarking methods, and IELTS2 (essay generation), which provides a long-form, open-
ended setting. For each dataset, we randomly sample 5,000 instances for training and 200
for evaluation without overlap.
Base Model π
We use Llama-3-8B-Instruct3 (Grattafiori et al., 2024) as the primary base
model for all main experiments. To assess the robustness to the choice of base model, we
additionally evaluate on the Qwen3 model family (QwenTeam, 2025) in Section 5.2.
Detector
We use the OpenAI Detector (Solaiman et al., 2019) as the primary detector
because it is widely used in prior work on machine-text detection (Nicks et al., 2024;
Kushnareva et al., 2024). Additionally, we evaluate robustness to alternative classifiers in
Section 5.2. We use AUROC as the evaluation metric for detection performance.
Evaluator
To investigate the effect of metric characteristics, we use ROUGE-L (reported as
a percentage in [0, 100]), a lexical overlap metric, for ELI5 and Multi-News. For IELTS, we
use an LLM-as-a-Judge score on a [0, 9] IELTS band scale to evaluate semantic quality.
Training / Evaluation
We fine-tune LLMs using DPO with LoRA (Hu et al., 2022) for
memory efficiency. We use a single fixed set of hyperparameters across all experiments for a
controlled comparison, including k = 5 candidate responses (following Meng et al. (2024))
and α = 0.5. For evaluation, models generate responses equal in number to the human
responses per sample (ELI5: 3, Multi-News: 1, IELTS: 1) to ensure fair metric computation.
Baselines
We compare PUPPET with five watermarking methods. Two are logit-based:
KGW (Kirchenbauer et al., 2023), which biases green-list token logits conditioned on the
preceding token, and Unigram (Zhao et al., 2024), which uses a fixed context-independent
green list. Three are sampling-based: EXPGumbel (Aaronson, 2023), which resamples
tokens via a seeded Gumbel distribution; SynthID (Dathathri et al., 2024), which selects
tokens through a tournament over multiple random scores; and K-SemStamp (Hou et al.,
2024b), which steers sentence-level generation toward a watermarked region in semantic
embedding space. Details of algorithms are provided in Section 6. We also report results for

Results
Table 1 presents the detection performance (AUROC) and task performance (ROUGE-L,
Judge) of Llama-3 models trained with PUPPET across three benchmarks. We also visualize
the token-level behavior of the responses using an ELI5 example in Figure 2. We draw two
key observations.
PUPPET improves both detection and task performance simultaneously.
Compared to
Vanilla, PUPPET improves AUROC by up to +12.3 points (IELTS: 87.0 →99.3), ROUGE-
L by up to +2.9 points (ELI5: 22.9 →25.8), and LLM-as-a-Judge score by up to +0.42
points (IELTS: 6.77 →7.19). This confirms that PUPPET jointly optimizes both objectives,
improving each relative to the Vanilla baseline.
PUPPET outperforms watermarking baselines in task performance while matching their
detectability.
Llama-3 models trained with PUPPET achieve task performance levels that
watermarked models cannot, with a gap of up to 6% on IELTS (SynthID: 6.76 vs. PUPPET:
7.19), while matching or surpassing them on detection. For example, PUPPET outperforms
KGW, the strongest watermarking baseline on detection, on 2 out of 3 benchmarks.

contribute to detection, and blue spans contribute to task performance. Concretely, red
spans are identified by SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP; (Lundberg & Lee, 2017))—

This provides intuitive evidence that DPO-based PUPPET leads the base LLM to acquire
features that benefit both detectability and task performance, as intended.
Note that the task performance degradation for watermarked models observed in prior
work is not consistently reproduced in our experimental settings. We conjecture that this
may be because recent LLMs can generate fluent text even under distributional constraints,
though we do not conduct a dedicated analysis to substantiate this claim. Regardless,
PUPPET’s contribution holds even in the absence of the reported degradation: PUPPET
actively improves task performance to levels that watermarking methods cannot reach.
5
Analysis
We conduct five analyses to further characterize PUPPET: (1) generalizability—whether
PUPPET transfers to out-of-domain tasks, (2) robustness—whether PUPPET holds up across
the different choices of base LLM, detector, and paraphrasing attacks, (3) efficiency—whether
PUPPET can be applied with modest data resources, (4) reward ablation—whether both
reward components are necessary for jointly optimizing both objectives, and (5) model
attribution—whether PUPPET enables distinguishing its outputs from those of other models.
5.1
Generalizability to Out-of-Domain Tasks
To assess whether PUPPET transfers beyond the tasks used during training, we evaluate the
trained models on tasks not seen during training. Table 2 reports the out-of-domain (OOD)
results (off-diagonal cells) alongside in-domain (ID) results (diagonal cells).
The results show that, even when evaluated on OOD tasks, PUPPET consistently improves
detection performance relative to the Vanilla baseline without degrading task performance.
For example, a model trained only on ELI5 improves AUROC on Multi-News from 92.8
to 97.3 and on IELTS from 87.0 to 94.9. This suggests that the detection-relevant features
learned by PUPPET transfer across tasks, rather than overfitting to the ID distribution.

5.2
Robustness
We assess PUPPET’s robustness along three axes: (i) the choice of base LLM, (ii) the choice
of detector, and (iii) adversarial paraphrasing attacks.
5.2.1
Base LLM Choice.
Table 3 reports results for three Qwen3 variants (QwenTeam, 2025) and examines robustness
to LLM choice along two sub-axes: model family and model size.
Model family.
Qwen3-8B is comparable in model size to Llama-3-8B-Instruct but belongs
to a different model family, allowing us to isolate the effect of model family. PUPPET
improves detection performance from 81.2 to 94.1 and task performance from 44.4 to 46.0
on average, demonstrating that its effectiveness generalizes beyond a single LLM family.
Model size.
We further evaluate Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-14B to assess PUPPET’s sensitivity
to model size.4 PUPPET consistently improves both objectives across all model sizes. The
detection gain is particularly large for Qwen3-14B (76.0 →97.4), where the stronger base
model is intrinsically harder to detect, yet PUPPET still closes most of the gap. On the task
side, PUPPET further improves each Vanilla baseline, regardless of size, demonstrating that
PUPPET complements rather than undermines the capabilities of larger models.
These results confirm that PUPPET’s effectiveness is not contingent on any particular model
family or model size. Full per-task results for the Qwen3 family are provided in Appendix B.
5.2.2
Detector Choice.
Table 4 shows results with FakeSpotAI5 and MAGE(Li et al., 2024), two detectors not used
in the main results, alongside the OpenAI Detector for reference. PUPPET consistently
improves both objectives across all detectors. Notably, FakeSpotAI already achieves high
detection performance on the Vanilla baseline, yet PUPPET further improves it while also
lifting task performance. This demonstrates that PUPPET’s gains are not confined to specific
detectors. Full per-task results are provided in Appendix C.

5.3
Training Efficiency
Even a method that achieves strong performance may have limited practical value if it
demands prohibitive data or computational resources. We therefore examine PUPPET’s
practicality along both dimensions. Figure 4 plots AUROC and task performance as a
function of the number of training samples seen for Llama-3 across all three benchmarks.
Across all benchmarks, both detectability and task performance rise sharply within the first
few thousand samples and plateau near the level achieved with the full training set. For
example, on ELI5, both performances converge within 1k–2k samples, with AUROC already
reaching 100.0 at 1k samples. This handful of DPO pairs represents a remarkably small
budget compared to large-scale DPO-based alignment pipelines such as OLMo3 (TeamOlmo,
2025), which train on 150K–200K pairs. Regarding compute, each training run completes
in approximately 1–2 hours on a single NVIDIA A6000 (48GB) GPU. These results confirm
that PUPPET is both data-efficient and computationally lightweight. The same trend holds
for Qwen3 (Appendix E).

both reward components are necessary: neither alone achieves strong performance across
both objectives. Moreover, α provides a practical knob: higher values favor detectability,
while lower values favor task performance. The same trend holds for Qwen3 (Appendix F).

As an exploratory analysis, we investigate the use of PUPPET for model attribution. PUPPET

class and Contrast model outputs as the negative (human) class, computing AUROC from
the OpenAI Detector’s machine-generated class likelihood. Table 5 shows Llama-3 results.

Related Work
Research on machine text detection can be broadly categorized into two directions: (1)
detectors: utilizing discriminative features of machine-generated text, and (2) watermarking:
embedding detectable features into text during generation.
Detectors
A standard approach involves training supervised classifiers on labeled datasets
of human-written and machine-generated text. RoBERTa (Liu et al., 2019) is widely used as
the base model (Solaiman et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2024b; Tulchinskii et al., 2023; Li et al.,
2024), and the RoBERTa-based OpenAI Detector (Solaiman et al., 2019) is widely used as a
benchmark in prior work (Nicks et al., 2024; Kushnareva et al., 2024).
A complementary, training-free paradigm exploits statistical properties of the genera-
tion process. DetectGPT (Mitchell et al., 2023) exploits the observation that machine-
generated text lies near local maxima of a model’s log-probability surface, so perturbations
lower its log-probability, whereas human-written text does not exhibit this behavior. Fast-
DetectGPT (Bao et al., 2024) achieves comparable accuracy at substantially lower cost by
replacing perturbation-based estimation with conditional probability curvature sampling.
Binoculars (Hans et al., 2024) achieves strong zero-shot detection by computing the ratio of
cross-perplexity and perplexity between two related models.
Watermarking
Watermarking methods embed detectable signals into LLM-generated text
and can be grouped into logit-based and sampling-based approaches.
Logit-based methods bias the token output distribution at generation time. KGW (Kirchen-
bauer et al., 2023) partitions the vocabulary into green and red lists conditioned on the
preceding token, and increases the logits of green-list tokens by a fixed δ. Unigram (Zhao
et al., 2024) simplifies this by using a fixed, context-independent green list, thereby making
it more robust to token-substitution attacks. Both methods introduce systematic distortions
into the output distribution, which has been shown to degrade task performance (Ajith
et al., 2024; Fu et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025a; Fernandez et al., 2023).
Sampling-based methods, in contrast, intervene at the token selection stage without directly
modifying logits. EXPGumbel (Aaronson, 2023) resamples tokens via a seeded Gumbel
distribution, and SynthID (Dathathri et al., 2024) selects tokens through a tournament
procedure over multiple random scores. K-SemStamp (Hou et al., 2024b) is a clustering-
based extension of SemStamp (Hou et al., 2024a), which steers sentence-level generation
toward watermarked regions in semantic embedding space. These methods are generally
less disruptive to the output distribution than logit-based approaches, but task performance
degradation can still be observed (Wang et al., 2025a).

Conclusion
We presented PUPPET, the DPO-based framework that trains an LLM to produce text that
is both highly detectable and performant on downstream tasks. By jointly optimizing
detectability and task performance, PUPPET matches watermarking methods in detection
while surpassing them on downstream tasks—a combination that prior methods, which
optimize only one objective at a time, cannot achieve. These gains generalize to out-of-
domain tasks and prove robust to the choice of base LLM, detector, and paraphrasing
attacks, all within moderate data and computational resources. Our exploratory analysis
further suggests that PUPPET opens the door to model attribution.
Two directions remain for future work: deeper mechanistic explanations of the acquired
detect-relevant features, and systematic hyperparameter tuning—including the relative
weighting of the two rewards—which may yield further gains. We hope this work encour-
ages research into jointly optimizing LLMs across multiple accountability objectives, thereby
contributing to more transparent deployment of language models.
Ethics Statements
Detection approaches, including PUPPET and watermarking, are still in the research stage.
Therefore, it is essential to use these techniques with utmost caution under high-stakes set-
tings where false positives (incorrectly identifying human-written text as machine-generated
text) may cause significant harm.
Reproducibility Statements
We release the PUPPET implementation on GitHub. The repository contains the experi-
mental code and configuration files used in this paper, enabling researchers to reproduce
our results. It also provides a refactored implementation to facilitate applying PUPPET to
researchers’ own models, data, and tasks.
